'''''Philodendron xanadu''''', [[Synonym (taxonomy)|synonym]] '''''Thaumatophyllum xanadu''''', is a perennial plant belonging to the arum family [[Araceae]]. It is native to south Brazil and Paraguay,<ref name=POWO_20011461-1/> but is widely cultivated as a [[landscape plant]] in tropical, subtropical, and warm temperate climates.

==History==
This plant was originally reported to be a selected chance seedling that arose in 1983 in a [[Western Australia]]n nursery. It was thought to be a sport or hybrid of ''[[Philodendron bipinnatifidum]]'', and named ''Philodendron'' 'Winterbourn' and protected under Plant Breeder Rights in Australia. It was also sold under the name ''P.'' 'Showboat'.{{cn|date=April 2025}} It was renamed 'Xanadu' by House Plants of Australia and released as their plant of the year in 1988.{{Citation needed|date=May 2025}} 

The cultivar name 'Winterbourn' was trademarked in the United States on January 19, 1988. That patent has since expired and there have since been substantiated claims that this plant is not a [[hybrid plant|hybrid]] or nursery-grown cultivar, but actually originated from seed collected from a wild plant in Brazil. This plant was described as ''Philodendron xanadu'' <small>Croat, Mayo & J.Boos.</small><ref>''Aroideana; Journal of the International Aroid Society'' 25: 63 (2002 publ. 2003)</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2620 |title=San Marcos Growers website |access-date=10 November 2014 |archive-date=10 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141110094038/http://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2620 |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Description==
===Growth habit===
''Philodendron xanadu'' is a perennial herb and forms dense clumps growing up to {{Convert|5|ft|m|abbr=off}} tall and {{Convert|5|ft|m|abbr=on}} wide.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Philodendron xanadu (Winterbourn Philodendron, Xanadu Philodendron) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox |url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/philodendron-xanadu/ |access-date=2025-05-08 |website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu |archive-date=13 October 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251013163718/https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/philodendron-xanadu/ |url-status=live }}</ref> It has glossy green, deeply dissected, lobed leaves up to {{convert|40|cm|0|abbr=on}} long by {{convert|30|cm|0|abbr=on}} wide. Its flowers have dark red spathes. It may occasionally produce aerial roots.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2620 |title=San Marcos Growers website |access-date=10 November 2014 |archive-date=10 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141110094038/http://www.smgrowers.com/products/plants/plantdisplay.asp?plant_id=2620 |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Distinguishing features===
''Philodendron xanadu'' is placed in the ''Meconostigma'' subgenus of ''Philodendron''. "It differs from all other species of ''Meconostigma'' in details of the sexual parts of its spadix, the shape of the leaf scars on the rhizomes, shape of leaf blade, intravaginal squamules, etc".<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://abrimaal.pro-e.pl/araceum/philodendron/xanadu.htm |title=Julius Boos, ''Philodendron xanadu'', Araceum website |access-date=10 November 2014 |archive-date=10 November 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141110094430/http://abrimaal.pro-e.pl/araceum/philodendron/xanadu.htm |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Cultivation==
''Philodendron xanadu '' is cultivated as a landscape plant in tropical, subtropical and warm temperate countries including warmer parts of the [[United States]], such as [[Florida]], Hawaii and [[California]], [[South Africa]], [[Australia]] and northern [[New Zealand]]. It is grown as a [[houseplant]] in cooler regions.

==Toxicology==
''Philodendron'' species are poisonous to vertebrates, but vary in their toxicity levels. They contain [[calcium oxalate]] crystals in [[raphide]] bundles, which are poisonous and irritating. The sap may cause skin irritation. Chewing and/or ingesting parts of the plant may result in severe swelling and compromised respiratory functions.
